claims.text: The initial sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles produced by PLD are nominally single-phase FCC.
Rapid quenching during PLD leaves the AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles with non-equilibrium atomic distributions.
For particles below 5 nm, the high surface-to-volume ratio makes surface-energy contributions dominate bulk mixing-entropy contributions.
Au and Cu are the low-surface-energy constituents of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
A surface-energy gradient drives Au and Cu from the particle interior to the exterior.
Surface-segregated Au and Cu subsequently evaporate during heating.
Surface lattice distortion lowers the activation energy for Au and Cu surface diffusion relative to bulk diffusion.
High defect density and under-coordinated surface atoms make surface diffusion anomalously fast.
The kinetic history of PLD accelerates segregation and evaporation by creating a defect-rich, kinetically trapped state.
Au/Cu evaporation causes particle shrinkage and reshaping from elliptical or icosahedral geometries toward spheres.
Au/Cu segregation and evaporation increase sharply at a critical temperature between 600 K and 800 K.
Preferential Au/Cu loss leaves a core enriched in Pt, Ni, and Co.
Differential evaporation associated with initial shape and local curvature widens the nanoparticle size distribution.
Initial icosahedral and truncated-octahedral particles have different segregation onset temperatures or rates.
For particles larger than 10 nm, bulk entropy dominates surface-energy contributions.
Above 10 nm, sluggish diffusion should prevent the segregation and evaporation observed in sub-5 nm particles.
High entropy and sluggish diffusion are generally associated with enhanced phase, chemical, and thermal stability in high-entropy alloys.
High entropy and sluggish diffusion stabilize AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles against segregation and coalescence up to their melting point.
A pressure below 10^-7 Torr prevents oxidation while permitting measurable evaporation.
Carbothermal-shock synthesis can provide HEA nanoparticle controls with sizes comparable to the proposed 3 nm specimens.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis calls segregation 'entropy-driven,' whereas the mechanism says the surface-energy term dominates and overcomes the bulk mixing-entropy term. These identify different primary thermodynamic drivers.

The proposed mechanism requires local lattice distortion, PLD-induced defects, under-coordinated atoms, and kinetic trapping, but the experiment is framed as testing whether surface-energy gradients alone explain phase separation. A surface-energy-only model does not directly test the full multicausal hypothesis.
The mechanism is declared strictly valid only below 5 nm, while the experiment includes a 5 nm condition. Behavior at exactly 5 nm is therefore not assigned to either the valid or invalid regime.

The intervention permits either vacuum or an inert atmosphere, while the specified conditions require high vacuum to allow evaporation. An inert atmosphere may impose different evaporation kinetics and is not reconciled with that requirement.
